rmt-2015-team-01.title: Along the diagonal
rmt-2015-team-01.body:
The first circle has center $(1,1)$ when $A=(0,0)$ and the second has center $(s-1,s-1)$, where $s=AB$. They are externally tangent, so the distance between centers is $2$: $\sqrt2\,(s-2)=2$, so $s=2+\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $2+\sqrt2$**

rmt-2015-team-02.title: Common prime factor
rmt-2015-team-02.body:
The gcd exceeds $1$ iff $a,b,c$ share a prime factor $p\le15$; since $a<b<c\le15$ are three distinct multiples of $p$, we need at least $3$ multiples of $p$ up to $15$: $p=2$ (7 multiples), $3$ (5 multiples), $5$ (3 multiples). Counts: $\binom73=35$, $\binom53=10$, $\binom33=1$. Triples counted twice would need a common factor $6$ or more (multiples of $6$: only $6,12$, so none). Total $35+10+1=46$.

**Answer: 46**

rmt-2015-team-03.title: Odd numbers lose
rmt-2015-team-03.body:
Claim: the player to move wins iff $N$ is even. Strong induction: $N=1$ loses. If $N$ is even, subtract $1$ to hand over the odd number $N-1$, a losing position. If $N$ is odd, every divisor $n$ is odd, so $N-n$ is even, a winning position for the opponent. So $N$ is a first-player win exactly when it is even; there are $1007$ even numbers among $1,\dots,2015$ (for $N=1$ the first player loses).

**Answer: 1007**

rmt-2015-team-04.title: Vieta
rmt-2015-team-04.body:
Let the roots be $r,s,rs$. Then $r+s+rs=2015$ and $n=-r\cdot s\cdot rs=-r^2s^2$. Adding $1$: $(1+r)(1+s)=2016=2^5\cdot3^2\cdot7$, which has $6\cdot3\cdot2=36$ divisors. We need $r,s\ge2$ (if $r=1$ then $rs=s$ and the roots are not distinct), so $1+r,1+s\ge3$; this excludes the divisors $1,2,1008,2016$, leaving $32$ ordered pairs, i.e. $16$ unordered pairs ($2016$ is not a square so $r\ne s$). Different pairs give different $rs$ (since $r+s=2015-rs$ determines the pair), hence $16$ different values of $n$.

**Answer: 16**

rmt-2015-team-05.title: Extinction probability
rmt-2015-team-05.body:
Starting with one robot, let $p$ be the probability that eventually no robots remain. Each robot's line dies out independently, so $n$ robots all die out with probability $p^n$. After the first morning there are $1,0,2,3$ robots with probability $\frac14$ each, so $p=\frac14\left(p+1+p^2+p^3\right)$, i.e. $p^3+p^2-3p+1=0=(p-1)(p^2+2p-1)$. The extinction probability is the smallest nonnegative root, $p=\sqrt2-1$ (the roots are $1$, $-1\pm\sqrt2$).

**Answer: $\sqrt2-1$**

rmt-2015-team-06.title: Regular tetrahedron
rmt-2015-team-06.body:
The centers form a regular tetrahedron of edge $2$. The smallest enclosing sphere is centered at the tetrahedron's center and touches each small sphere at its far point, so its radius is $1+R$, where $R$ is the circumradius of the tetrahedron. For an edge $a$, $R=\frac{\sqrt6}4a=\frac{\sqrt6}2=\sqrt{\frac32}$. (Check: the vectors from the center to the vertices have pairwise angle $\varphi$ with $\cos\varphi=-\frac13$, and $2^2=2R^2(1+\frac13)$ gives $R^2=\frac32$.)

**Answer: $1+\sqrt{\frac32}$**

rmt-2015-team-07.title: Tangency condition
rmt-2015-team-07.body:
By symmetry the center is $(0,r)$ and the circle touches the $x$-axis. Its upper half is $y=r+\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$. Tangency to the parabola means $r+\sqrt{r^2-x^2}=2-x^2$ has a double solution. Squaring: $r^2-x^2=(2-r-x^2)^2$, which gives $x^4+(2r-3)x^2+(4-4r)=0$. This is a quadratic in $x^2$ with a double root when the discriminant vanishes: $(2r-3)^2-4(4-4r)=0$, i.e. $4r^2+4r-7=0$, so $r=\frac{-1+2\sqrt2}2$ (positive root).

**Answer: $\dfrac{2\sqrt2-1}2$**

rmt-2015-team-08.title: Solve the tangency system
rmt-2015-team-08.body:
A common point $(x,y)$ with equal slopes satisfies $e^{ax}=\frac1a\ln x$ and $ae^{ax}=\frac1{ax}$. Dividing the first relation by the second gives $\ln x=\frac1{ax}$..., i.e. $a=\frac1{x\ln x}$. The slope condition $ae^{ax}=\frac1{ax}$ then reads $e^{ax}=\frac1{a^2x}$, so $ax=-\ln(a^2x)$. With $L=\ln x$ and $ax=\frac1L$ this becomes $\frac1L=L+2\ln|L|$. The function $\varphi(L)=L+2\ln|L|-\frac1L$ has $\varphi'(L)=\left(1+\frac1L\right)^2\ge0$ on each of $L>0$ and $L<0$, so it has exactly one zero on each: $L=1$ and $L=-1$. Then $x=e$, $a=\frac1e$, or $x=\frac1e$, $a=-e$.

Check: $a=\frac1e$: $f(x)=e^{x/e}$ is tangent to $y=x$ at $x=e$ (value $e$, slope $1$), and since $g=f^{-1}$ they are tangent there. $a=-e$: $f(x)=e^{-ex}$ passes through $(\frac1e,\frac1e)$ with slope $-1$, and $g=f^{-1}$ also has slope $-1$ there, so they are tangent. In each case this is the only tangency.

**Answer: $a=\frac1e$ or $a=-e$**

rmt-2015-team-09.title: Scale factor and pentagon area
rmt-2015-team-09.body:
Let the small pentagon have side $x$. Each diagonal of the large pentagon has length $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ and is cut by the two diagonals crossing it into pieces $y,x,y$, so $2y+x=\varphi$. Also a vertex $A$ and the far crossing point $P$ on a diagonal satisfy $AP=AB=1$ (triangle $ABP$ has angles $36^\circ,72^\circ,72^\circ$), which gives $x+y=1$. Hence $y=\varphi-1=\frac{\sqrt5-1}2$ and $x=\frac{3-\sqrt5}2$.

The area of a regular pentagon with side $d$ is $\frac14\sqrt{25+10\sqrt5}\,d^2$. With $d=x$, $d^2=\frac{7-3\sqrt5}2$, so the area is $\frac{7-3\sqrt5}8\sqrt{25+10\sqrt5}$. Squaring, $(7-3\sqrt5)^2(25+10\sqrt5)=(94-42\sqrt5)(25+10\sqrt5)=250-110\sqrt5$, so the area equals $\frac18\sqrt{250-110\sqrt5}\approx0.251$.

**Answer: $\dfrac18\sqrt{250-110\sqrt5}$**

rmt-2015-team-11.title: Integral recurrence
rmt-2015-team-11.body:
Let $f(n)$ be the expected number of turns on an uncovered interval of length $n$. For $n<2$ at most one unit interval fits, so $f(n)=\lfloor n\rfloor$ (i.e. $0$ for $n<1$, $1$ for $1\le n<2$). For $n\ge1$, the first interval's left endpoint $r$ is uniform on $[0,n-1]$, leaving two independent intervals of lengths $r$ and $n-1-r$. So $f(n)=1+\frac2{n-1}\int_0^{n-1}f(r)\,dr$ for $n\ge2$.

For $2\le n\le3$: $\int_0^{n-1}f=n-2$, so $f(n)=1+\frac{2(n-2)}{n-1}=3-\frac2{n-1}$. For $n=4$: $\int_0^3f=\int_1^2 1\,dr+\int_2^3\left(3-\frac2{r-1}\right)dr=1+3-2\ln2=4-2\ln2$, so $f(4)=1+\frac23(4-2\ln2)=\frac{11-4\ln2}3$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{11-4\ln2}{3}$**

rmt-2015-team-12.title: Trigonometric substitution
rmt-2015-team-12.body:
Write $a_n=\sin^2(\pi\theta_n)$ with $\theta_n\in[0,\frac12]$. Then $a_{n+1}=4\sin^2\pi\theta_n\cos^2\pi\theta_n=\sin^2(2\pi\theta_n)$, so $\theta_n$ is $2^n\theta_0$ (mod the symmetries of $\sin^2$). The condition $a_q=a_0$ means $\sin^2(2^q\pi\theta)=\sin^2(\pi\theta)$, i.e. $2^q\theta\equiv\pm\theta\pmod1$, so $\theta=\frac k{2^q-1}$ or $\theta=\frac k{2^q+1}$. In $[0,\frac12]$ the first family gives $k=0,1,\dots,2^{q-1}-1$, that is $2^{q-1}$ values, and the second gives $k=1,\dots,2^{q-1}$, that is $2^{q-1}$ values. The two families share no value, since $\gcd(2^q-1,2^q+1)=1$ and $\theta=0$ appears only in the first. As $a=\sin^2\pi\theta$ is injective on $[0,\frac12]$, there are $2^q$ periodic points $a_0\in[0,1]$ in total, one of which is $a_0=0$. Removing it leaves $2^q-1$; for $q=2015$ this is $2^{2015}-1$.

Sanity check: the $q$-th iterate is a polynomial of degree $2^q$, so $x-f_q(x)$ has at most $2^q$ roots, and the count above attains that bound.

**Answer: $2^{2015}-1$**

rmt-2015-team-13.title: Symmetry and degree
rmt-2015-team-13.body:
Write $x_0=2^{1/5}$, $x_1=2^{2/5}$, $x_2=2^{3/5}$, $x_3=2^{4/5}$ and $F=\sum abc\,(x_0+ax_1+bx_2+cx_3)^4$. $F$ is a polynomial of degree $\le4$ in the $x_i$ and is symmetric under swapping any two of them (relabel $a,b,c$ and the sign changes accordingly). If $x_0=0$, the terms for $(a,b,c)$ and $(-a,-b,-c)$ have equal fourth powers but opposite signs $abc$, so they cancel: $F=0$. By symmetry $F=0$ whenever any $x_i=0$, so each $x_i$ divides $F$ and $F=Kx_0x_1x_2x_3$ for a constant $K$. The coefficient of $x_0x_1x_2x_3$ in $(x_0+ax_1+bx_2+cx_3)^4$ is $4!\,abc$, so $K=\sum abc\cdot24\,abc=8\cdot24=192$. Hence $F=192\cdot2^{(1+2+3+4)/5}=192\cdot2^2=768$.

**Answer: 768**

rmt-2015-team-14.title: Parametrize the deltoid
rmt-2015-team-14.body:
Take $p$ on the small circle initially at the tangency point. When the center of $A$ has polar angle $\varphi$ (at distance $\frac23$ from the origin), the small circle has rolled so that $p$ is at $\left(\frac23\cos\varphi-\frac13\cos2\varphi,\ \frac23\sin\varphi+\frac13\sin2\varphi\right)$. The curve is a deltoid (hypocycloid with three cusps). Differentiating, the speed squared is $\frac49\left[(\sin2\varphi-\sin\varphi)^2+(\cos\varphi+\cos2\varphi)^2\right]=\frac49\left[2+2\cos3\varphi\right]=\frac{16}9\cos^2\frac{3\varphi}2$, so the speed is $\frac43\left|\cos\frac{3\varphi}2\right|$. The length is $\int_0^{2\pi}\frac43\left|\cos\frac{3\varphi}2\right|d\varphi=\frac43\cdot\frac23\int_0^{3\pi}|\cos u|\,du=\frac89\cdot6=\frac{16}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{16}{3}$**

rmt-2015-team-15.title: Lagrange interpolation
rmt-2015-team-15.body:
For $i=1,\dots,4$ let $p_i(z)=\prod_{j\ne i,\,j\le4}(x_j-z)$. The $i$-th term of the expression is $\dfrac{x_5^3\,p_i(-1/x_5)}{p_i(x_i)}$, because $x_jx_5+1=x_5\left(x_j+\frac1{x_5}\right)$. The polynomial $P(z)=\sum_{i=1}^4\frac{p_i(z)}{p_i(x_i)}$ has degree at most $3$ and equals $1$ at the four distinct points $x_1,\dots,x_4$ (as $p_i(x_j)=0$ for $j\ne i$), so $P\equiv1$. Hence the whole expression equals $x_5^3$. To maximize it, minimize $x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4$ over distinct positive integers: the minimum is $1+2+3+4=10$, giving $x_5=90$ (distinct from $1,2,3,4$). The maximum is $90^3=729000$.

**Answer: 729000**
